name: Compressing PDF files
title: Compress PDFs online: choose a quality preset or diagnose a large file
metaTitle: Compress PDF Online: Choose a Quality Preset
metaDescription: Compare three PDF compression presets, keep text searchable when needed, and learn when to split a large file or use a sharing link.
intro: PDFs can be large because of images, fonts, metadata or saved document structure. PrintxPDF offers three compression presets: Light keeps the text layer, while Medium and Strong turn pages into images. There is no custom DPI or grayscale control. These guides explain the trade-offs, how to diagnose a large file and when a scanner setting, page split or sharing link is a better fit.
answer: In PrintxPDF, choose Light to keep text selectable. Medium and Strong turn pages into images and can reduce detail. The tool has no custom DPI or grayscale controls, so test on a copy and keep the original. Split the file or share a link if compression is not suitable.

posts.title: How to compress a PDF file for free
posts.metaTitle: How to Compress a PDF File for Free
posts.metaDescription: Compress a PDF in your browser with Light, Medium or Strong. Learn which keeps searchable text, which turns pages into images, and how to check the result.
posts.answer: Open the browser-based compressor and choose Light to keep text selectable, or test Medium or Strong on a copy if image-only pages are acceptable. Size reduction depends on the PDF. PrintxPDF does not offer custom DPI or grayscale settings.

body.x: Compression can rewrite document structure, change image data, or do both. The right option depends on what is inside the PDF and what you need to preserve. PrintxPDF's browser tool presents three presets rather than separate technical controls.
The two kinds of PDF compression

**Structural compression** changes how PDF data is stored without rasterizing page content. A structural pass may reduce overhead, but its operations and savings depend on the tool and source file. PrintxPDF's **Light** preset writes object streams and updates standard document metadata; it does not promise custom image downsampling or a fixed percentage reduction.

**Image-based compression** renders pages as pictures. It can reduce some scans, but searchable text becomes pixels and fine detail can be lost. PrintxPDF's **Medium** and **Strong** presets use this approach; they do not expose a DPI or JPEG-quality selector.

body.caption: Common compression operations and the trade-offs to check.
head: Method
What it changes
What to expect
Reversible
rows: Depends on fonts and the tool
Deletes unreferenced data left by edits
Reduces pixel dimensions to a target DPI
Can reduce size, but removes searchable text
Depends on the source and quality setting

body.x: Compress a PDF in your browser

items.x: Open [Compress PDF](/tools/compress-pdf) and choose a file. This tool runs in your browser, so the file is not uploaded to our server. Keep an original copy before changing anything.
Select **Light** if you need to search, select or copy text. The size change varies; a clean or already-compressed PDF may shrink very little.

items.h: Check whether images are the problem
items.x: If Light barely changes the size, the file may be dominated by images or already-compressed data. Consider whether converting pages into pictures is acceptable before using a stronger preset.

Choose **Light** to keep text selectable. **Medium** and **Strong** render each page as an image, so text is no longer searchable or selectable and fine detail may change. The tool does not expose a DPI setting; compare a copy before using a stronger preset.
Open the compressed file and zoom to 200 percent on the smallest text on the page. Compression artefacts show up around letter edges before they show anywhere else.
Save the compressed copy under a new name. You cannot un-downsample an image, so the original is your only fallback.

body.x: Compare Light, Medium and Strong in your browser. Keep the original and inspect the result before sharing.
Choosing a resolution

body.caption: DPI targets and what they are for. Sizes are per A4 page of a colour scan.
head: Target DPI
Pixel size (A4)
Approx. size per page
Use for
rows: Archival masters, fine artwork, OCR of tiny print
Screen reading, email, most business documents

body.x: These DPI figures are a reference for preparing scans, not controls in PrintxPDF's compressor. To change scan resolution, use scanner or image software before making the PDF. Choose based on the smallest text, expected print size and any OCR needs.
What lossless compression actually removes

items: **Unused font glyphs.** A full CJK or large OpenType font can be 5-20 MB. If your document uses 40 characters of it, subsetting stores 40 glyphs.
**Orphaned objects.** Editing tools frequently write new objects and leave the old ones behind. Nothing references them, but they still occupy bytes.

**Old revisions.** PDF supports incremental saving, where each save appends to the end of the file instead of rewriting it. A file saved thirty times can carry twenty-nine dead copies of its earlier self.
**Duplicate resources.** The same logo embedded once per page becomes one shared object.
**Uncompressed streams.** Some generators write page content streams with no Flate compression at all. Simply zipping them can halve a file.
**Bloated metadata.** XMP packets, thumbnails and structure trees left behind by design tools.

body.x: When compression does almost nothing

A clean, text-only PDF may already be compact, so compression can make little difference. A much smaller output may have been rasterized, which can remove searchable text. Check the result by selecting text or using Ctrl+F to find a visible word.

Rewriting a signed or certified PDF can invalidate its digital signature. Preserve the signed original. If a smaller unsigned copy is acceptable, make a separate copy and check the recipient's requirements first.
Compressing on the desktop
If you prefer local tools, three work well:

items: **macOS Preview**, File → Export, then set Quartz Filter to "Reduce File Size". It is aggressive and slightly crude, but it is already installed.
**Ghostscript**, free, scriptable and the engine behind many online compressors.

body.x:
# 150 DPI, good for email and screen reading
gs -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dCompatibilityLevel=1.7 \
   -dPDFSETTINGS=/ebook -dNOPAUSE -dQUIET -dBATCH \
   -sOutputFile=small.pdf big.pdf

# /screen = 72 dpi, /ebook = 150 dpi, /printer and /prepress = 300 dpi
If it is still too big

Compression has limits. If a scan is still too large, split it into parts or use an approved sharing link. See [reducing a PDF for email](/blog/compress/reduce-pdf-file-size-for-email) for current provider guidance, and [why your PDF is so large](/blog/compress/why-is-my-pdf-so-large) to diagnose the source.
Too big even after compressing? Split it into chapters or page ranges instead.

faqs.q: Does compressing a PDF reduce quality?
faqs.a: Light does not rasterize pages, so text remains selectable. Medium and Strong convert pages into images and can reduce fine detail. Keep the original and compare the output before sharing.

faqs.q: How much can a PDF be compressed?
faqs.a: There is no reliable percentage for every PDF. A text document, a scan and a photo-heavy file respond differently, and already-compressed PDFs may barely shrink. Compare output size and readability.

faqs.q: Is it safe to compress a PDF online?
faqs.a: Compress PDF processes the file in your browser and does not upload it to our server. This statement applies to this tool; other services may use a different processing method.

faqs.q: Why did compressing my PDF make it bigger?
faqs.a: A PDF can contain data that does not compress further, or an image-based result may not be smaller for that source. PrintxPDF returns the Light result instead when Medium or Strong would produce a larger file.

faqs.q: Can I compress a PDF without losing the text layer?
faqs.a: Yes. Choose **Light** in PrintxPDF to keep the text layer. **Medium** and **Strong** render pages as images. Test the result with text selection or search, and keep the original.

posts.title: How to reduce a PDF file size for email
posts.metaTitle: Reduce a PDF for Email: Compress, Split or Share
posts.metaDescription: Compare compression, page extraction, splitting or a link for a large PDF. Check the sender and recipient limits before sending.
posts.primaryKeyword: reduce pdf file size for email
posts.answer: Check your mail provider's current limit first. PrintxPDF offers Light compression, which keeps text selectable, and Medium or Strong, which turn pages into images. The tool has no custom DPI or grayscale controls; split the file or use an approved sharing link if compression is not enough.

body.x: An email bounce may only say "message too large." Limits depend on the sender, recipient and account type, so check the provider's current help page before changing a document. Here are common published limits and safer next steps.
Attachment limits by service

body.caption: Published sending limits checked October 2026. Workspace and business accounts may have administrator-set limits.
head: Service
Stated limit
Larger files
rows: Gmail can replace oversize attachments with a Google Drive link
Share through OneDrive or another approved service
Check with the administrator or use an approved file-sharing link
20 MB; Mail Drop supports messages up to 5 GB
Mail Drop links are available for up to 30 days
Use a file-sharing link if the recipient can access it
Share using Proton Drive or another service
Varies by administrator and recipient system
Check both organizations' rules before sending

body.x: Email encoding can add roughly one-third to an attachment's transmitted size, but providers do not all describe or enforce their limits the same way. Leave room for the message and check the sender's interface and the recipient's rules rather than relying on a universal safe-size calculation.

The recipient may have a lower limit than the sender, especially at work or school. If you cannot confirm it, a sharing link with the right access permissions is often more reliable than a large attachment.
Get the file under the limit

items.x: Right-click the file → Properties on Windows, or Get Info on macOS. Use the size in MB, not the "size on disk".

Open [Compress PDF](/tools/compress-pdf) and choose **Light**. It keeps the text selectable and avoids converting pages to images, though the file-size reduction depends on the PDF. Keep the original.

items.h: Decide whether image-only pages are acceptable
items.x: The tool's **Medium** and **Strong** options turn each page into an image. They do not offer a custom DPI setting, and the resulting text may no longer be searchable or selectable. Test a copy and inspect fine print before using either level.

items.h: Use a separate image workflow only if needed
items.x: Compress PDF does not include a grayscale or per-image resolution control. If the scan is still too large, adjust a copy with your scanner or image software, or split the document instead.
Confirm the new size, open the file once to make sure it still reads properly, then attach it.

body.x: Compare Light, Medium and Strong on a copy. Medium and Strong convert pages to images, so inspect text and detail before sharing.
Split it instead

A large report may not shrink enough without losing detail. Splitting is an alternative: send chapters separately or share only the requested pages. Use [Extract Pages](/tools/extract-pages) for a specific range, or [Split PDF](/tools/split-pdf) for separate files. See [splitting a large PDF for email](/blog/split/split-large-pdf-for-email).
Send a link instead of a file

items: **Google Drive**, in Gmail, use the Drive button or accept Gmail's prompt for an oversize attachment. Choose the narrowest sharing permission that lets the intended recipient open the file.
**OneDrive**, in Outlook, Insert → Link → Browse this computer, then choose "Upload and share". Recipients outside your tenant may need the link set to "Anyone".
**iCloud Mail Drop**, Apple Mail can offer this when a message exceeds the provider limit. Apple allows Mail Drop messages up to 5 GB; links can be downloaded for up to 30 days.
For other services, use a file-sharing option approved for the recipient and check its current size, expiry and access rules.

body.x: A shared link also fixes the version problem. If you find a mistake after sending, you replace the file at the link. An attachment sits in the recipient inbox forever in its wrong version.
Before you send anything

A PDF carries the author name, the software that made it, and often the full path of the folder it was saved in. If the file is going outside your organisation, [strip the metadata](/blog/privacy/remove-metadata-from-pdf) first. It takes a few seconds and costs nothing in file size.

If the file is a scan, adjust resolution or colour in the scanner settings before creating the PDF. Choose settings that keep small text readable, and save a new copy rather than overwriting the original. See [why your PDF is so large](/blog/compress/why-is-my-pdf-so-large) for other causes.

faqs.q: What is the maximum PDF size I can email?
faqs.a: Limits vary by service and account type. Personal Gmail and Yahoo Mail publish a 25 MB outgoing limit, Outlook.com publishes a 20 MB email limit, and iCloud Mail allows 20 MB or up to 5 GB through Mail Drop. Work and school administrators may set different limits. Check current provider guidance and leave room for message overhead.

faqs.q: Why does my 20 MB PDF fail to send on a 25 MB limit?
faqs.a: Email encoding can add roughly one-third to an attachment's transmitted size, but providers handle their published limits differently. The recipient's account may also have a lower cap. Check both sides or send a permitted sharing link.

faqs.q: How do I email a PDF that is 100 MB?
faqs.a: Use a sharing service approved by the recipient, such as Google Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox, and set access for the intended person. If attachments are required, ask the recipient for a per-message limit and split the PDF into files that leave room below that limit.

faqs.q: Does zipping a PDF make it smaller?
faqs.a: Usually very little, because many PDF contents are already compressed. ZIP is more useful for bundling several files than shrinking one PDF. Compare the archive size before sending it.

faqs.q: What DPI should I use for a PDF I am emailing?
faqs.a: There is no single DPI target for every document. Choose scan resolution based on the smallest text, print size and whether OCR is needed. PrintxPDF's compressor does not expose a DPI setting.

posts.title: How to compress a PDF without losing quality
posts.metaTitle: Compress a PDF Without Losing Quality
posts.metaDescription: Learn what lossless PDF compression preserves, when image-based compression affects text, and how to choose settings for a scan without risking the original.
secondaryKeywords: reduce pdf size without quality loss
posts.answer: To preserve selectable text with PrintxPDF, choose Light. Medium and Strong render pages as images and may reduce detail. The compressor has no custom DPI control; change scan resolution in scanner or image software, keep the original, and compare the result.

body.x: "Without losing quality" means two different things depending on what is inside your PDF, and most compression advice confuses them. A text document and a scanned document need opposite treatment.
What lossless actually means in a PDF
Lossless is a precise technical claim: decompress the result and you get the original bytes back. In PDF terms, only a handful of operations qualify.

body.caption: Genuinely lossless operations versus operations that only look lossless.
head: Operation
Truly lossless
What it costs you
rows: Nothing, unless someone later edits the text and needs a missing glyph
Nothing. Removes only data no page points to
The entire text layer and all searchability

body.x: The last row is the trap. Some "compressors" convert every page to a JPEG and wrap the images back in a PDF. The file gets dramatically smaller and looks fine at 100 percent zoom, but the text is now a picture: unsearchable, unselectable, unusable for screen readers. Always press Ctrl+F on the result and search for a word you can see on screen.
Text documents: lossless is usually enough
A PDF exported from Word, Google Docs or LaTeX is mostly vector text and a few images. There are no pixels to throw away, so the entire saving comes from structure. Realistic expectations:

items: A clean 20-page report exported today: **5-15 percent**. It was already efficient.
The same report after twelve rounds of edits and comments: **30-60 percent**, because incremental saves left old revisions inside the file.
A document embedding a full CJK or large icon font: **can be dramatic**, since subsetting a 12 MB font down to the glyphs actually used is a single huge win.
A document assembled by [merging](/tools/merge-pdf) ten sources: **20-40 percent**, because deduplication collapses the ten copies of the same logo into one.

body.x: Scans: pick a DPI and accept the trade

A scanned page is a picture. Reducing its pixels can save space but loses detail. The right resolution depends on the destination and smallest text. The DPI table below is general scanning guidance, not a setting in PrintxPDF's compressor.

body.caption: What each DPI target actually looks like.
head: DPI
Readable on screen
Readable printed
OCR accuracy
Verdict
rows: Overkill unless archiving or scanning tiny print
The safe default when the file will be printed
Best balance for text scans destined for email
Fine for reading, risky if you still need to OCR

body.x: If the PDF needs OCR, start with a clear source scan and run [OCR](/tools/ocr-pdf). Then choose **Light** in PrintxPDF to keep the searchable text layer. **Medium** and **Strong** turn pages into images, so they remove selectable and searchable text. Check the result with Ctrl+F and keep your original. See [how to OCR a scanned PDF](/blog/ocr/how-to-ocr-a-scanned-pdf).
The colour mistake that costs the most
Most people scan black text on white paper in 24-bit colour because that is the scanner default. That stores three channels for a page that has one channel of information. Two better options:

items: **Greyscale (8-bit)**, one third of the data, keeps the soft edges that make text look natural, and handles pencil marks, stamps and signatures well. This is the right default for scanned contracts.

**Bitonal (1-bit)**, one twenty-fourth of the data. With CCITT Group 4 or JBIG2 encoding, a full page of text can be 20-60 KB. Perfect for clean printed text; terrible for anything with photographs, shading or a coloured letterhead.

body.x: A safe procedure

items.x: Copy the file before you touch it. Everything below is reversible only if you still have the source.
In [Compress PDF](/tools/compress-pdf), choose **Light**. It does not rasterize pages and keeps text selectable. Note the new size; if it meets your needs, stop here.
A screen-only copy may need less resolution than a print or OCR copy. This tool does not change DPI, so set resolution when scanning or preparing an image copy.
If scanner or image software offers resampling, work from the original scan and export a separate copy. Recompressing lossy images repeatedly can add visible artefacts.
Zoom in on the smallest text and on any diagonal line or fine table rule. Artefacts appear there first, long before they show in body text.
Ctrl+F for a visible word. If it is not found, the tool rasterised your pages, discard the result.

body.x: Use Light to keep text selectable; keep the original before trying image-based compression.

If Light does not reduce the size enough and image-based compression would hurt readability, split the file or use a sharing link. See [reducing a PDF for email](/blog/compress/reduce-pdf-file-size-for-email) for current provider guidance.

faqs.q: Is there such a thing as truly lossless PDF compression?
faqs.a: Yes. Some structural operations do not alter visible page content, but savings depend on the PDF and the tool. PrintxPDF's Light preset does not rasterize pages and does not guarantee a fixed reduction percentage.

faqs.q: What DPI should I compress a PDF to?
faqs.a: It depends on the smallest text and intended use. 150 to 300 DPI can be a useful scan range, but print and OCR requirements vary. PrintxPDF does not have a DPI selector; change scan settings before creating the PDF.

faqs.q: Will compressing a PDF break the OCR text?
faqs.a: It depends on the preset. **Light** does not rasterize pages, so text stays selectable. **Medium** and **Strong** turn each page into an image, which removes selectable text. OCR first if needed, choose Light, and check with Ctrl+F before sharing.

faqs.q: Why does my compressed PDF look blurry when I zoom in?
faqs.a: An image-based preset may reduce fine detail, especially when you zoom in. Keep the original and compare at the size the recipient will read or print. The tool does not let you select an exact DPI.

faqs.q: Does compressing a PDF twice make it smaller?
faqs.a: A second lossless pass gains nothing. A second lossy pass makes it smaller but stacks JPEG artefacts, and the damage compounds visibly. Always compress the original once at the setting you actually need.

posts.title: Why is my PDF file so large? 8 reasons
posts.metaTitle: Why Is My PDF So Large? 8 Causes and Fixes
posts.metaDescription: Eight things that make a PDF huge: scanned pages, unsubsetted fonts, duplicated images, incremental saves, uncropped photos, form fields and colour profiles.
posts.primaryKeyword: why is my pdf so large
posts.answer: A PDF is usually large for one of eight reasons: it is a scan stored as images, images are embedded at full resolution, fonts are embedded whole instead of subset, resources are duplicated per page, saves were incremental, images are cropped only visually, forms and attachments are attached, or colour profiles and transparency are heavy.

body.x: A four-page memo should be about 100 KB. If yours is 40 MB, something specific is wrong, and it is almost always one of the eight causes below. Work down the list, the first three account for the large majority of oversized files.
1. It is a scan, not a document

The single most common cause. If your PDF came from a scanner, a copier or a phone camera, every page is a photograph. A 600 DPI colour scan of one A4 page is 4960 × 7016 pixels, 35 megapixels, which is more than most cameras produce. Twenty pages of that is easily 100 MB.

**Fix:** downsample to 150-200 DPI and switch colour scans of black text to greyscale. On the scanner itself, set 200 DPI greyscale as your default for documents. Reserve 300 DPI colour for photographs and artwork.
2. Images are embedded at their original resolution

You dropped a 6000-pixel-wide photo from your phone into a Word document and scaled it to two inches. On screen it looks like a small picture; inside the file it is still 6000 pixels wide, which works out to 3000 DPI. You are storing a hundred times more image data than the page can ever show.

**Fix:** resize images to their display size before placing them. A 2-inch-wide image at 300 DPI needs 600 pixels. In Word, Picture Format → Compress Pictures → 220 ppi does this for the whole document at once.
3. Fonts are embedded in full instead of subset

PDF embeds fonts so the file renders identically everywhere. Well-behaved generators embed only the glyphs used, a subset. Badly-behaved ones embed the entire font file. A Latin font is 100-500 KB, but a CJK font covering Chinese, Japanese and Korean can be 5-25 MB. Embed three of those in full and you have a 60 MB file with nothing but text in it.
**Fix:** use a PDF optimizer that explicitly supports font subsetting, then inspect font properties in a desktop PDF reader. PrintxPDF's Light preset does not perform font subsetting.
4. The same resource is stored many times

A letterhead logo placed on all 80 pages should be one object referenced 80 times. Some generators, and almost every "merge these files" workflow that does not deduplicate, store 80 separate copies. The same happens with background images, watermarks and repeated table graphics.

**Fix:** deduplication is part of a proper structural compression pass. It is also why a merged document is often much larger than the sum of its parts until you compress it. See [merging PDF files](/blog/merge/how-to-merge-pdf-files).
5. Every save was an incremental update

PDF allows a writer to append changes to the end of the file rather than rewriting it. This is fast and it preserves digital signatures, so annotation tools use it constantly. The cost is that every previous version stays in the file. A document annotated across thirty sessions can carry twenty-nine dead copies of itself.
**Fix:** a full rewrite, sometimes called "Save As" rather than "Save", or "linearise", collapses the history into a single current version.

Old revisions are a privacy problem too. If someone redacted a paragraph and saved incrementally, the original text may still sit in an earlier revision. [Remove metadata and flatten](/blog/privacy/remove-metadata-from-pdf) before sharing anything sensitive.
6. Images are cropped visually, not actually

Cropping in InDesign, PowerPoint or Word usually sets a visible frame over the image rather than deleting the hidden pixels. Crop a 20-megapixel photo down to a thin banner and the file still carries all 20 megapixels. The same applies to images placed partly off the edge of the page.
**Fix:** in Word and PowerPoint, Compress Pictures has a "Delete cropped areas of pictures" checkbox. Tick it. In InDesign, use Package or export with image downsampling enabled.
7. Forms, annotations, attachments and scripts

items: **Form fields** carry appearance streams, a stored rendering for each visual state of each field. A 200-field form can add several megabytes.
**Embedded file attachments.** PDF can carry arbitrary files inside it. A spreadsheet attached to a report is invisible in the page view and fully counted in the file size.
**Annotation appearance streams** from highlighting and commenting tools.
**JavaScript** for form validation, plus the fonts those form fields reference.

body.x: **Fix:** if the form is filled and finished, [flatten it](/tools/flatten-pdf). Flattening bakes the field values into the page and removes the interactive layer, which usually cuts a completed form substantially and also stops anyone editing the answers.
8. Colour profiles, transparency and vector overload

Print-ready files carry weight you do not need on screen: embedded ICC colour profiles for CMYK output, transparency groups flattened for older viewers, and vector artwork with tens of thousands of paths. A detailed map or CAD drawing exported as vectors can be 30 MB with no images at all.

**Fix:** export for screen rather than for press, which drops the CMYK profiles. For a monstrous vector illustration, converting that one page to a 300 DPI image is often a 95 percent saving with no visible difference on screen.
Diagnosing your own file

items.x: Open the PDF and drag across a paragraph. If nothing highlights, it is a scan, cause 1, and you can stop reading here.
Under 100 KB per page is a normal text document. 100 KB - 1 MB usually means images. Over 1 MB per page is a scan or a full-resolution photo problem.
File → Properties → Fonts in any full PDF viewer. Anything not marked "Embedded Subset" is cause 3.
Split the file and compare the parts. One 25 MB page among forty 80 KB pages points straight at a single oversized image or vector drawing.
Whatever the [compressor](/tools/compress-pdf) removes without touching images was structural waste, causes 3, 4 and 5.

body.caption: Quick diagnosis by symptom.
head: Symptom
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Save As, or run a structural rewrite
Merged file bigger than its parts
Resize the image, delete cropped areas

body.x: Start with a lossless pass, it tells you how much of your problem is structural.

faqs.q: Why is my PDF bigger than the Word document it came from?
faqs.a: Word stores images compressed and fonts by reference. A PDF embeds the fonts and often stores images re-encoded at full resolution so the file renders identically everywhere. Use Word Compress Pictures at 220 ppi before exporting to close most of the gap.

faqs.q: Why did my PDF get bigger after I added a comment?
faqs.a: Annotation tools save incrementally, appending the change to the end of the file instead of rewriting it. Each session adds another layer. Doing a Save As, or running a structural compression pass, collapses them back into one version.

faqs.q: How big should a normal PDF be?
faqs.a: Roughly 20-100 KB per page for text with a few images. 100 KB - 1 MB per page for image-heavy documents. Over 1 MB per page almost always means scanned pages or photos embedded at their original camera resolution.

faqs.q: Does deleting pages reduce PDF file size?
faqs.a: Only if the tool rewrites the file. Some editors mark pages as removed but leave the objects in place. Delete the pages, then run a compression pass so the orphaned objects are actually dropped.

faqs.q: Can a PDF be large with no images at all?
faqs.a: Yes. Fully embedded CJK fonts, complex vector artwork such as maps or CAD exports, hundreds of form fields with appearance streams, and embedded file attachments can all produce a very large PDF with nothing but text and lines on the page.

posts.title: Gmail and Outlook PDF attachment limits: what to do
posts.metaTitle: Gmail and Outlook PDF Attachment Limits
posts.metaDescription: Check your mailbox and recipient limits, then choose whether to compress or split a PDF or use an approved sharing link. Limits vary by account and workplace.
posts.answer: To email a PDF that is too large, first check your mail provider’s current attachment limit, then compress the PDF and inspect whether the text and images remain clear. If it is still too large, split it into smaller files or use the recipient-approved file-sharing service. Do not assume ZIP will shrink already-compressed images.

body.x: A PDF can be too large because its pages contain high-resolution photos or scans, because it carries unused objects, or because it has many pages. The right fix depends on which is responsible. Check the mail provider’s current limit before changing the document, since limits and organization policies can vary.
A safe sequence to reduce the attachment

items.x: Look up the attachment limit for your mail account and the recipient’s organization. Leave room for email encoding overhead; a file close to the stated maximum can still fail.
Use [Compress PDF](/tools/compress-pdf), then inspect small print, photographs and scanned signatures at normal viewing size.

items.h: Remove pages the recipient does not need
items.x: Extract a useful page range with [Extract Pages](/tools/extract-pages), but keep the complete original separately.

items.h: Split if compression is not enough
items.x: Split the PDF into clearly named parts and make sure each part stays under the recipient’s limit.
For very large or confidential documents, use the organization’s approved cloud sharing method and restrict access as needed.

body.x: Try reducing the PDF size in your browser and check the output before attaching it.
Why a ZIP archive may not help

PDFs often already compress their text and images internally. Putting a PDF into a ZIP can therefore save little or nothing. A PDF containing uncompressed scans may shrink more, but a photo-heavy PDF may not. Compare the sizes before sending.
Choose quality based on what the PDF is for

head: Document
What to protect
Possible approach
rows: Lower image resolution cautiously and inspect each page
Keep a high-quality master; share a separate smaller copy
Do not modify the authoritative signed original

body.x: Compression or editing can invalidate a digital signature. Keep the signed original untouched and do not treat a compressed copy as the authoritative signed record.

If the recipient only needs a few pages, extract those pages instead of sending the whole file. If the PDF contains sensitive information, use the right access controls and avoid sending passwords in the same email as the attachment.

Email limits are not always the only constraint. A company gateway may impose a lower maximum than the sender mailbox, and a recipient may block certain file types or encrypted archives. If delivery fails after compression, compare the exact error with the attachment size and ask whether a secure share link is accepted. Avoid renaming a compressed copy over the source until you have checked its pages and text. For records with signatures, approvals or legal retention requirements, keep the original separately and treat the compressed version as a convenience copy only.

faqs.q: How do I email a PDF that is too large?
faqs.a: Check the current limit, compress the file, remove pages the recipient does not need, then split it or use an approved file-sharing service if it remains too large. Inspect the compressed file before sending.

faqs.q: Will zipping a PDF make it smaller?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but often only slightly because PDFs already compress many streams and images. Test the ZIP size rather than assuming it will help.

faqs.q: Can I compress a digitally signed PDF?
faqs.a: Editing or optimizing a signed PDF may invalidate its signature. Preserve the original signed file and ask the signer or records owner before creating a modified copy.

faqs.q: How small should a PDF be for email?
faqs.a: Use the current limit for your mail provider and account, and leave margin for encoding overhead and recipient limits. There is no single size that is safe for every mail system.
